entities.name: Church of Ireland
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Church of Ireland, established by act of the Irish Parliament in 1536-1537 as part of Henry VIII's Reformation, is the Anglican church in Ireland — a province of the Anglican Communion with approximately 375,000 members across both Ireland and Northern Ireland, making it a minority church (2% of the Republic of Ireland's population) after having been the established (state) church of Ireland for 333 years (1536-1869). The Church of Ireland's disestablishment (1869 Act) under Gladstone — removing its state privileges in a predominantly Catholic country — was a landmark moment in the separation of British imperial church policy from Irish religious reality.

The Church of Ireland was imposed through the 16th-century Tudor conquest: Acts of Supremacy made Henry VIII head of the church in Ireland; monasteries were dissolved; Catholic worship was progressively restricted. However, unlike England and Scotland where Protestantism took hold, Ireland remained overwhelmingly Catholic — making the Church of Ireland (with 10% or less of the population) the established church over a Catholic majority for three centuries, collecting tithes from Catholics for the Protestant establishment.

The 1869 Irish Church Act (Gladstone's first great Irish reform) disestablished the Church of Ireland — ending compulsory tithes, removing bishops from the House of Lords, and returning church endowments. The disestablishment was a model for subsequent British imperial church reforms. Today the Church of Ireland is a cross-border church (Ireland and Northern Ireland), making it one of the few all-Ireland institutions that operates across the Republic-Northern Ireland border. Saint Patrick's Cathedral Dublin (Anglican) and Christ Church Cathedral Dublin (Anglican) remain among Ireland's most visited historic sites.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Church of Ireland — established over a Catholic majority for 333 years and then disestablished in Gladstone's landmark 1869 reform — is the clearest example in British history of a state church imposed on a population that never converted to it, and the 1869 disestablishment remains the model for church-state separation in British constitutional history.
